summary: Northern Morocco was under Umayyad governors only from c. 708 until the Berber Revolt of 740, after which it broke away from the caliphate. The 10th century saw the Fatimids and the Umayyads of Córdoba fight over it through local proxies, and Córdoba ruled some coastal towns directly. Real caliphal rule over almost all of Morocco came through the Almoravids (who recognised the Abbasids, c. 1050s–1147) and then the Almohads, a counted caliphate (1147–1269). Later dynasties (Marinids, Wattasids, Saadians, Alaouites) did not recognise an outside caliph. The one exception is Abd al-Malik (1576–78), who had the khutba read in the Ottoman sultan's name.

units.label: Northern Morocco, Fez and Tafilalt (al-Maghrib al-Aqṣā; Sijilmāsa)
units.who: Umayyad governors (Tangier) until the Berber Revolt. In the 10th century, Fatimid and Córdoban-Umayyad direct posts and proxies. Then the Almoravids (recognised the Abbasids) and the Almohad caliphate directly.
units.dates: c. 708–740 Umayyad direct (Tangier); 909 and 958–60 Fatimid campaigns (Sijilmasa, Fez); Córdoba direct at Melilla 927, Ceuta 931, Tangier 951, and Fez via the Maghrawa from 987/88; Almoravid c. 1055 (Sijilmasa) to early 1080s (Fez) until 1147; Almohad 1147–1269
units.notes: Umayyad rule here was short: Musa ibn Nusayr took Tangier c. 705–708, and the Berber Revolt of 740 permanently ended Umayyad control. Under the Idrisids the land was ruled by Muslims but by no caliph. Fatimid and Córdoban control in the 10th century was patchy and contested; Córdoba directly held coastal towns (Melilla, Ceuta, Tangier). The Midrarids of Sijilmasa are listed as nominal Abbasid and then Fatimid vassals. The firm caliphal period is Almoravid (Abbasid-recognising) and Almohad rule.
units.uncertain: Ceuta and Melilla are not in these admin-1 polygons; I used them only as evidence for Córdoba's footing on this coast. The exact length of direct Córdoban rule in Fez (via al-Mansur's governors) was not confirmed in an opened page. The 'nominal vassal' status of the Midrarids comes from the Wikipedia infobox, not checked further.

units.who: Almoravids (recognised the Abbasids), then the Almohad caliphate directly
units.dates: Almoravid conquest c. 1058–1060 to 1147; Almohad 1147–1269 (Barghawata finally eliminated 1149)
units.notes: For about three centuries the Tamesna coast between Salé and Safi was ruled by the Barghawata, whose heterodox religion mixed Islamic and local Berber elements. They recognised no caliph and resisted Córdoba, the Fatimids and the Almoravids; Ibn Yasin was killed fighting them in 1058/59. Caliphal rule begins only with the Almoravid conquest and is completed by the Almohads.
units.uncertain: I could not confirm whether the Umayyad governors (708–740) ever actually administered Tamesna, so I have not claimed it. The Barghawata's exact borders (Bou Regreg to the Oum Er-Rbia, or to Safi) are only approximate.

Before the Almoravids, I found no verified evidence of caliphal administration here.

units.label: Wadi Nun and the northern Saguia el-Hamra (Nūl Lamṭa)
units.who: Almoravids (recognised the Abbasids), possibly the Almohads
units.dates: probably 1050s–1147 (Almoravid); not confirmed

units.notes: The Wadi Nun lay on the Almoravid corridor between the Sahara and the Sous, so it was very probably inside the Almoravid realm. I could not open a page that confirms this. In the early modern period the Ma'qil and Tekna tribes of the Wadi Nun gave allegiance to Moulay Ismail (1678), but by 1767 Morocco's treaty with Spain admitted it did not control the Tekna. The Es-Semara part of this province is really Western Saharan Saguia el-Hamra; Smara was only founded in 1869 and was Ma al-Aynayn's religious capital from 1902.

If that rule is rejected, this unit drops to islamic_state_ruled. The southern (Smara) part of the polygon has a different, Western Saharan history.

units.label: Western Sahara inside Morocco's admin-1 (Sāqiyat al-Ḥamrāʾ and Wādī al-Dhahab / Río de Oro)
units.who: No verified caliphal administration. This is the Sanhaja homeland of the Almoravid movement, but the Almoravids' Abbasid recognition dates to Yusuf ibn Tashfin's northern state.

states.n: Moroccan sultans (allegiance of some tribes only)

units.notes: The Almoravid movement grew from the Sanhaja tribes of this desert. Their rule there was a tribal confederation, not an administration with governors. Later, Hassaniya-speaking tribes sometimes gave allegiance (bay'a) to Moroccan sultans. In 1975 the ICJ found ties of allegiance with only some tribes, and no Moroccan or Mauritanian territorial sovereignty. This is a strictly historical classification, not a statement on today's sovereignty dispute.
units.uncertain: It is unclear whether the Saharan Almoravids under Abu Bakr ibn Umar (to 1087) used the Abbasid name; the opened pages tie Abbasid recognition to Yusuf ibn Tashfin. Rating this as an 'Islamic state ruled' land is generous: in practice it may be closer to tribal autonomy with occasional allegiance.

summary: The east (Constantinois, Zab) belonged to Ifriqiya. It was ruled by Umayyad and then Abbasid governors, by the Aghlabids for the Abbasids, and from 909 by the Fatimids, whose movement started among the Kutama of Petite Kabylie. The west and centre were lost to the caliphate in 740 and went to the Rustamid Ibadi imamate and the Idrisids. They came back under caliph-linked rule through the Fatimids and Zirids/Hammadids, the Almoravids and the Almohads. From the 16th century the Ottoman Regency of Algiers (from 1516/1519 to 1830) administered the Tell. The Saharan oases were only tributary or autonomous, and the far south (Ahaggar, Tindouf) was never really ruled.

units.label: Constantinois and Petite Kabylie (western Ifrīqiyah; Kutāma country)
units.who: Umayyad then Abbasid governors. Then the Aghlabids for the Abbasids, the Fatimids directly, the Zirids for the Fatimids, and the Hammadids (alternating Abbasid/Fatimid recognition). Then the Almohad caliphate, and the Ottoman Beylik of Constantine.

units.notes: This is the most solidly caliph-ruled part of Algeria. Aghlabid towns included Mila and Setif. The Fatimid da'wa began among the Kutama near Ikjan (893). Béjaïa was the Hammadid capital. In the Ottoman era the Beylik of Constantine was the Regency's most populous province, under a bey appointed by the dey.
units.uncertain: Some mountain districts (e.g. Babors, parts of Petite Kabylie) were probably only loosely controlled in every period; I did not check this district by district.

units.label: Aurès, Zab and Hodna (al-Zāb; Ṭubna, al-Masīla)
units.who: Umayyad and Abbasid governors at Tobna (capital of the Zab), Aghlabids for the Abbasids, the Fatimids (founded M'Sila 927), Zirids/Hammadids (Qal'at Bani Hammad in M'Sila), Almohads, the Ottoman Beylik of Constantine

units.notes: Tobna (Batna province) was the governors' capital of the Zab for about two centuries, so the lowlands were firmly administered. The Aurès mountains were the base of the Kahina's resistance (defeated c. 701) and later of Ibadi Hawwara rebels against the Fatimids (947), so the high Aurès were probably more loosely held. Biskra had a Hammadid governor and later belonged to the Ottoman Beylik of Constantine.
units.uncertain: How far each regime controlled the interior Aurès massif, as opposed to the Zab and Hodna plains, was not checked.

units.label: Greater Kabylia (land of the Zwāwa; Kingdom of Kuku)
units.who: The Ottoman Regency of Algiers held forts (bordjs) in the Sebaou and neighbouring valleys. Before that, Hammadid/Almohad reach into the mountains is unclear.
units.dates: Ottoman forts 18th c. (Tazarart 1710s, Boghni 1724); Kuku a tributary 'feudatory' of Algiers from the mid-16th c.
units.notes: The high Kabyle mountains largely governed themselves. The Kingdom of Kuku allied with, fought and later paid modest tribute and troops to Ottoman Algiers. units.label: Western Tell / Oranie (Tilimsān)
units.who: Umayyad conquest (708) until 740. Then the Maghrawa of Ziri ibn Atiyya under Córdoban Umayyad protection, the Almoravids (Abbasid recognition), the Almohad caliphate directly, and the Ottoman Regency (Beylik of the West).

Ottoman rule began at Tlemcen in 1551, but Oran stayed Spanish until 1792.

summary: Tunisia was the heart of Ifriqiya and the most continuously caliph-ruled land in the Maghreb. Its rulers in turn were Umayyad governors from Kairouan (670), the Aghlabids for the Abbasids (800–909), the Fatimids directly (909–973) and the Zirids for the Fatimids. The Zirids switched to the Abbasids around 1048. After that came the Almohads (1159–1229) and the Ottomans (1574–1881). The Hafsids (1229–1574) recognised no outside caliph and claimed the caliphate themselves from 1253.

units.label: Northern and central Tunisia (core of Ifrīqiyah: Qayrawān, Tūnis, al-Mahdiyya)
units.who: First a Rashidun raid (Sufetula 647). Then Umayyad and Abbasid governors at Kairouan, the Aghlabids for the Abbasids, the Fatimid caliphs (capital Mahdia), and the Zirids for the Fatimids and then for the Abbasids. Later the Almohad caliphate, and the Ottoman pashas, deys and beys.
units.dates: 647 raid (tribute, no occupation); 670–800 Umayyad/Abbasid direct (Carthage 698; Kharijite seizure of Kairouan 745/758 aside); 800–909 Aghlabid; 909–973 Fatimid direct; 973–c.1048 Zirid for the Fatimids, then for the Abbasids to 1148/1160; 1159/60–1229 Almohad; 1574–1881 Ottoman
units.notes: The 647 battle of Sufetula (Sbeitla, Kassérine) was a Rashidun raid bought off with tribute, not a conquest. Lasting rule began with Kairouan in 670. The Norman Kingdom of Africa held Mahdia and some coastal towns (1148–1160) and Spain held Tunis 1535–1574, so the coast had breaks. Under the Husainids Ottoman suzerainty became largely formal.
units.uncertain: The exact dates of Norman and Spanish coastal enclaves within each province were not mapped. The Zirid switch to the Abbasids is given as 1041–1051 in the opened source.

summary: Cyrenaica (Barqa) and Tripoli were conquered by Amr ibn al-As under the Rashidun caliph Umar in 642–643. Cyrenaica then followed Egypt (Umayyad, Abbasid, Fatimid, Ayyubid, Mamluk) and Tripolitania followed Ifriqiya (Aghlabid, Fatimid, Zirid, Almohad, Hafsid). The Ottomans held Tripoli from 1551 and Benghazi from 1578, directly or through the Karamanlis (1711–1835). The Fezzan was raided in 642 and 666–67 and then ruled by local Muslim dynasties (Ibadi Banu Khattab, Kanem, Awlad Muhammad); the Awlad Muhammad were tributary to the Ottomans, who ruled directly from 1842. Kufra was never really under any caliph; the Sanusiyya made it their centre from 1895.

The Karamanlis were hereditary rulers under nominal Ottoman suzerainty.

From the 1570s–80s the Awlad Muhammad gave allegiance to the Ottoman sultan, with a garrison, and direct Ottoman rule came only in 1842. The Rustamid imamate's influence reached Zawila (9th c.).

summary: No caliph ever administered Mauritania. It was ruled instead by Muslim powers that did not formally recognise a caliph. In the north, the Almoravid movement rose among the Sanhaja in the 1040s–1050s, with Azougui in the Adrar as its first capital; Abu Bakr ibn Umar ruled the Saharan wing until he died in Tagant in 1087. The south-east was in Ghana's and then Mali's sphere (Walata a Mali garrison town). The Senegal valley had Muslim Takrur (from c. 1035) and the Futa Toro Imamate (1776). From the 17th century the Hassaniya emirates (Trarza, Brakna, Adrar, Tagant) ruled until French protectorates (1902–1912).

summary: Only the southern rim of Kazakhstan (Isfijab/Sayram, Taraz, Otrar, Jand, Semirechye) came under caliph-recognising dynasties: the Samanids, the Karakhanids after c.1001 and the Khwarazmshahs. No caliphal governor ever ruled the northern, central or western steppe, whose first Muslim rulers were the Islamised Golden Horde (from 1313), the Nogai Horde and the Kazakh khans. The Kimek-Kipchak and Oghuz confederations were not Muslim states, and the Qara Khitai (1130s-1211) were non-Muslim overlords. Russia absorbed the steppe between the 1730s and 1860s.

summary: Almost all of Uzbekistan was conquered by the Umayyads under Qutayba b. Muslim (705-715) and then ruled directly by Umayyad and Abbasid governors, though the Turgesh rolled much of it back between 720 and 738. Outlying principalities (Khwarazm, Chaghaniyan, Ushrusana, Shash, Ferghana) were first tributaries and came under Abbasid and Samanid rule between 751 and 893. After the Mongols, Muslim states that did not recognise a caliph ruled: the Chagatayids, Timurids, Shaybanids and the khanates of Bukhara, Khiva and Kokand. Russia conquered it between 1865 and 1876.

summary: Southern Turkmenistan (Merv, Nasa, Abivard, Sarakhs) was part of Khurasan and fell to the Rashidun caliphate in 651, staying under caliphal and caliph-recognising rule until the Mongols. Khwarazm (Dashoguz) and Dihistan (Balkan) were first tributary or briefly conquered and later ruled by caliph-recognising dynasties. After 1220, Muslim states that did not recognise a caliph followed: the Golden Horde, Timurids, Khiva, Bukhara and Iran. The Turkmen tribes were independent until the Russian conquest of 1881-1885.

summary: No Umayyad or Abbasid governor ever ruled Kyrgyz territory except the Ferghana valley, which the Samanids governed for the caliph from 819. The Chu valley, Talas and Issyk-Kul came under Muslim rule through the Karakhanids, whose capital was Balasagun and who recognised the Abbasids from about 1001, until the non-Muslim Qara Khitai took over in 1134. Later Muslim states were Moghulistan (Muslim khans from 1354) and Kokand (early 19th c.), separated by long Kyrgyz tribal and Dzungar periods. Russia took the north in the 1850s-60s and Kokand in 1876.

summary: Northern Tajikistan (Panjikant, Ushrusana, Khujand) and Khuttal in the south were conquered and ruled under the Umayyads and Abbasids, Ushrusana only from 822 and Khuttal fully from 750-751, and then by the Samanids and Ghaznavids. Karategin and the Pamirs (Gorno-Badakhshan) kept their own princes or mirs and came under larger Muslim states (Bukhara, Afghanistan) only in the 1870s-1890s. Bukhara ruled most of the country under Russian protection until 1920-21.

summary: Western Afghanistan (Herat, Sistan) and the north (Balkh/Tokharistan) were taken into the Rashidun and Umayyad caliphates in the 650s-710s and governed by caliphal governors. The east and south-east (Kabul, Zabulistan, Ghazni) resisted for two centuries under the Turk/Hindu Shahis and the Zunbils, paying tribute at times, and came under lasting Muslim rule only with the Saffarids (870) and Ghaznavids (late 10th c.), who recognised the Abbasid caliph. Ghor was Islamised only in the 11th century and later ruled by the Abbasid-recognising Ghurids. Nuristan (Kafiristan) was never ruled by a caliphate or recognising dynasty; it was conquered and converted by Amir Abdur Rahman Khan in 1895-96.

summary: Sind and Multan were conquered by the Umayyads in 711-713 and governed by caliphal governors, then by local dynasties that read the khutba for the Abbasids (Habbarids of Mansura, Banu Munabbih of Multan) or, at Multan, the Fatimids. Makran was entered under Umar (644) and was the launching base for 711. Northern Punjab, the Peshawar valley and Islamabad's area stayed under the Hindu Shahis until the Ghaznavid conquest (1001-1026), and the Ghaznavids recognised the Abbasid caliph. Gilgit-Baltistan and Azad Kashmir were never under a caliphate; they came under local Muslim dynasties, the Kashmir Sultanate and the Mughals from the 14th-16th centuries, then Sikh and Dogra (non-Muslim) rule from 1819-1840 until 1947.

units.notes: Makran (coast and Kech) was entered under Umar (23/644) and served as the Umayyad route to Sind in 711, so it counts as directly ruled, though Umar barred further advance and control later loosened. Inner Baluchistan (Turan/Qusdar) is less clear: Iranica says it is not named in the early conquest accounts. Caliphal rule there is shown only through local rulers reading the Abbasid khutba in the 10th century, before it became a Ghaznavid tributary. The northern Pashtun belt (Quetta-Pishin, Zhob) and the Marri-Bugti hills followed Kandahar's or tribal history.

units.notes: Islam arrived through Sufi missionaries from Kashmir and Central Asia from the 14th century (Baltistan largely Nurbakhshi by the 17th century; Hunza Ismaili). It was then ruled by local Muslim dynasties, with brief Kashmir Sultanate campaigns and Mughal intervention. Muslim rule ended with the Sikh and Dogra conquests of 1839-1870, which lasted until the 1947 Gilgit revolt.

Muslim rule came with the Kashmir Sultanate (from 1339) and especially the Mughals, under whom local Muslim chiefs founded Mirpur (c. 1640) and Muzaffarabad (1646). Afghan (Durrani) rule followed until the Sikh conquest of 1819 and Dogra rule (1846-1947).
